questions.q: What is the veil of ignorance exercise?
a: Designing a society without knowing your place in it
Judging a villain without knowing the facts
Hiding your identity while arguing online
Imagining life without any moral rules
questions.why: Lesson 1 says you create a society, then enter it with no control over your position.

questions.q: What does the exercise reveal about morality?
a: Moral labels are shaped by your environment
Most people prefer an unfair society
Moral rules are the same everywhere
Rules are impossible to create
questions.why: Lesson 1 says we would design a fair society, showing how arbitrary our labels can be.

questions.q: Why do people dislike Kim Dotcom?
a: He changed how people consume media
He was convicted of supporting terrorism
He stole money from his investors
He refused to use the internet
questions.why: Lesson 2 says he forced media companies to rethink their business and they resented it.

questions.q: Why is Hitler often seen as more evil than Stalin?
a: Familiar details make his crimes feel worse
He killed far more people than Stalin
Stalin's crimes were never documented
Hitler was never held responsible
questions.why: Lesson 3 says familiarity makes Hitler relatable, so his crimes feel worse despite Stalin's higher toll.

questions.q: What does the summary conclude about judging villains?
a: Feelings do not always match the facts
Facts always determine our feelings
The worst villain is always the most familiar
History judges everyone accurately
questions.why: Lesson 3 says how we feel about evildoers can diverge from what the facts show.
